label: Bears, moose, cougars and other wildlife
summary: Bears follow food smells to garbage, feed, fruit and carcasses, so rotting food in dead freezers, stores and dumpsters draws them: hungry in spring, eating 20–23 hours a day in autumn. Moose and elk charge in rut or with young, cougars treat children and pets as prey, and dogs cause most bites.
signs: Spring (late March to mid-May): bears leave their dens while food is scarce and work valley bottoms, roadsides and winter-killed animals
Late summer and autumn: bears gorge to fatten for winter, and males with food around can stay awake past Christmas
Fresh bear tracks or diggings, a large dead animal, or ravens and magpies gathering over a kill that a bear or cougar may be guarding
Moose: bulls in rut from mid-September to December, cows with calves from mid-May to June. Ears pinned back, neck hair raised, mouth smacking, stomping, head swaying and short charges mean back off
Elk: bulls in rut (August to October) can attack without warning, and cows defend their calves aggressively from mid-May to the end of June

Cougars: widespread in BC, in Alberta's wooded, rocky country and river valleys, and now and then in Manitoba's southern river valleys. Most active at dawn and dusk; tracks show no claw marks, and kills are covered with debris
A coyote that doesn't run off: most flee before you see them, and the habituated ones are the dangerous ones
do: Keep at least 100 m from bears, cougars and wolves and 30 m from moose, elk and deer. Make noise and travel in a tight group
Store food, garbage, pet food and feed indoors or in sealed bear-resistant bins, away from where you sleep, and keep fruit, bird seed and compost out of reach
Bear close by: stop, stay calm and don't run. Gather your group, talk calmly, back away slowly, and get into a building or vehicle if one is near

Bear spray: when a bear that keeps coming is within about 5–7 m, wind at your back if you can, spray 1–2 second bursts at its face, aimed a little low so it runs into the cloud. Then back away and leave the area

A bear that attacks after a surprise, or near cubs or food: if it makes contact, lie on your stomach, legs apart, hands clasped behind your neck, and stay still until it leaves. If it keeps going, stalks you or comes at night, fight back hard at its face

Cougar or coyote: pick up small children, face it, make yourself big and loud, use bear spray if it comes close, and back away slowly. If it attacks, fight back at its eyes and face with anything you have
Moose: keep a tree, vehicle or building between you; if one knocks you down, curl into a ball and protect your head and neck
dont: Don't run from a bear, cougar or coyote, and don't turn your back on it
Don't play dead with a cougar, or with a bear that is stalking or hunting you
Don't go near a large carcass or a heap of spoiled food: something may be feeding on it or guarding it
Don't feed wildlife or leave food out: animals that link people with food lose their fear of people
Don't spray bear spray on yourself or your gear (the smell attracts bears), don't spray into the wind, and don't trust a can that has expired or been left in a hot or freezing vehicle
Don't let your dogs roam: they can provoke bears and draw cougars, coyotes and wolves, which may attack them. Keep away from stray dogs as well
ppe: Bear spray labelled for deterring bear attacks, at least 225 g, with a current expiry date, ideally one per person, carried in a hip or chest holster rather than in a pack
A can lasts only about 8–10 seconds in all and reaches about 10 m, but is dependable only at close range (Parks Canada gives 5 m); wind, rain and freezing temperatures weaken it
firstAid: Bites and scratches: wash straight away with soap and plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes, and don't cover the wound. A bat touching bare skin counts: wash there too
A bite or scratch from any mammal that might have rabies, or any contact with a bat, needs rabies treatment before symptoms start: once they appear, rabies is almost always fatal

Bear spray on you: get to fresh air. Flush skin with cold water and mild soap, then pat dry. For eyes, put your head under water and open them every few seconds, and take out contact lenses. Don't rub or use creams; it should ease within 30–45 minutes
For head, neck and crushing injuries from a mauling or a moose, see Fall from height and Crush and pinch points
